content: Henna, also known as Hina (Lawsonia inermis), is a flowering plant and the only species in the genus Lawsonia, belonging to the family Lythraceae. It is native to tropical and subtropical regions of Africa, southern Asia, and northern Australasia, thriving in semi-arid zones. Henna grows as a tall shrub or small tree, reaching heights of 2 to 6 meters. The plant is glabrous and multi-branched, with branchlets tipped with spines. Its leaves are 5–2 cm long, acuminate, and have depressed veins on the dorsal surface. During rainy periods, the plant grows rapidly, producing new shoots, but growth slows during dry or cool intervals, during which the leaves gradually yellow and fall. Henna flowers have four sepals, a 2 mm calyx tube with 3 mm spread lobes, and obovate petals that are white or red. The stamens are inserted in pairs on the rim of the calyx tube. The ovary is four-celled, with an erect style up to 5 mm long. The fruits are small, brownish capsules, 4–8 mm in diameter, containing 32–49 seeds per fruit, and they open irregularly into four splits. The concentration of lawsone, the dye molecule in henna leaves, is inversely related to the number of seeds in the fruits. Henna produces a red-orange dye molecule called lawsone, which has a strong affinity for bonding with proteins. This property makes it useful for dyeing skin, hair, fingernails, leather, silk, and wool. Henna grows best in tropical savannah and arid zones, between latitudes 15° and 25° N and S, from Africa to the western Pacific rim. It produces the highest dye content in temperatures between 35°C and 45°C and does not thrive in areas where minimum temperatures fall below 11°C. Temperatures below 5°C are fatal to the plant. The lawsone molecule is primarily concentrated in the leaves, with the highest levels found in the petioles. Products marketed as black henna or neutral henna are not derived from henna but may come from indigo (Indigofera tinctoria) or Cassia obovata and may contain unlisted dyes and chemicals. Henna is commercially cultivated in western India, Pakistan, Morocco, Yemen, Iran, Sudan, and Libya. The Pali district of Rajasthan, India, is currently the largest henna production area, with over 100 henna processors operating in Sojat City. Henna has been used for body art and hair dye since the Bronze Age and has recently experienced a resurgence in popularity due to improvements in cultivation, processing, and the spread of traditions from henna-using regions. The word henna originates from the Arabic name Hina for Lawsonia inermis. In the Bible, henna is referred to as Camphire in the Song of Songs and Song of Solomon. In the Indian subcontinent, it is known as Mehndi in North India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh. In Arabic-speaking countries in North Africa and the Middle East, it is called Hina. In Telugu, it is known as Gorintaaku, and in Tamil, it is called Marudhaani, where it is often used as ground fresh leaves rather than dried powder. Henna is used in various festivals and celebrations, particularly by women and children, and is typically left on overnight, lasting for a month or more depending on the plant quality and application method. Henna has numerous traditional and commercial uses, including as a dye for hair, skin, and fingernails, as a preservative for leather and cloth, and as an antifungal agent. Historical records indicate its use as a hair dye in Indian court records around 400 CE, in Rome during the Roman Empire, and in Spain during the Convivencia. It is also mentioned in ancient medical texts such as the Ebers Papyrus (16th century BCE, Egypt) and by Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya (14th century CE, Syria and Egypt) as a medicinal herb. In Morocco, henna is used to dye and decorate wool, drumheads, and other leather goods. It also repels some insect pests and mildew. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not approved henna for direct application to the skin but has approved it unconditionally as a hair dye. It can only be imported for this purpose, although enforcement is rare. Products labeled as black henna often contain para-phenylenediamine (PPD), a chemical that can cause severe allergic reactions, blistering, and permanent scarring. Henna itself cannot produce a black stain on the skin in a short time. PPD is illegal for use on the skin in Western countries, but enforcement is lax. When used in hair dye, PPD concentrations must be below 6%, and instructions warn against scalp contact and require quick rinsing. Black henna pastes often contain PPD concentrations of 10% to 60% and are left on the skin for extended periods, leading to widespread use in tourist areas despite the risks. Allergic reactions to natural henna are rare, but some individuals may react to essential oils or lemon juice used in the henna mix. Lawsone can cause hemolytic oxidation in individuals with G6PD deficiency, potentially leading to severe hemolytic crises or fatal outcomes, especially in children. Henna body art is created by applying henna paste to the skin, where the lawsone molecule migrates into the outermost skin layer, producing a red-brown stain. Whole, unbroken henna leaves do not stain the skin until the lawsone molecules are released by crushing the leaves with a mildly acidic liquid. Dried, ground, and sifted henna leaves are more suitable for creating intricate body art. Commercial henna powder is made by drying and milling the leaves into a fine powder, which is then mixed with acidic liquids like lemon juice or strong tea. Essential oils containing monoterpene alcohols, such as tea tree, eucalyptus, cajeput, or lavender, enhance the staining properties. The henna mix must rest for 6 to 12 hours to release the lawsone, after which it is applied to the skin using traditional or modern tools. The paste is left on the skin for several hours, during which the lawsone molecules migrate deeper into the skin. The paste is often sealed with a sugar/lemon mixture to prevent cracking and enhance the final color. Once removed, the stain appears orange but darkens over three days to a reddish-brown. The darkest and longest-lasting stains occur on the palms and soles due to their thick skin layers. Steam or warmth can further darken the stain, while chlorinated water and soaps may interfere with the darkening process. The stain fades as the skin exfoliates, shedding the stained cells. Henna has been used for body art in social and ceremonial contexts since the late Bronze Age in the eastern Mediterranean. Ancient texts and artifacts suggest its use in marriage and fertility celebrations, with women adorning themselves with henna in preparation for significant events. The Night of the Henna is a traditional celebration observed by various cultural and religious groups, including Jews, Muslims, Hindus, and Zoroastrians, to mark joyous occasions such as weddings, births, and festivals. Henna was believed to bring blessings (Barakah) and was applied for luck, joy, and beauty. Bridal henna traditions are particularly elaborate, with intricate patterns symbolizing joy and good fortune. Modern innovations in henna processing and application have increased its artistic potential, and talented henna artists can command high fees for their work. Henna businesses thrive in many countries, providing socially acceptable and lucrative work for women, especially during festivals and large weddings. Pre-mixed henna pastes may contain illegal additives to alter stain color or intensity, such as silver nitrate, carmine, pyrogallol, disperse orange dye, and chromium. These substances can cause allergic reactions, chronic inflammation, or delayed allergic responses to hairdressing products and textile dyes. Medical reports have identified heavy metals like nickel, cobalt, chromium, lead, and mercury in some henna tattoos, posing additional health risks. Black henna is a misnomer, as it often contains PPD rather than henna. PPD-based pastes can cause severe allergic reactions, permanent scarring, and lifelong chemical sensitivities. Tourists are particularly vulnerable to these injuries, as reactions often occur days after application. PPD sensitivity is lifelong, and exposure to synthetic hair dyes can become life-threatening. Natural henna does not cause these injuries and remains safe for use as a hair dye.
